AMOEBIC_LIVER_ABSCESS.title: Amoebic liver abscess (pus pocket in the liver)

items: An amoeba (a single-celled parasite called Entamoeba histolytica) can spread from the gut to the liver and form a pocket of pus (abscess).
It is most often seen in people who have lived in or travelled to areas where amoebiasis is common.
Fever and pain in the upper right side of the belly, where the liver is.
Jaundice (yellow skin and eyes) is rare.
Diarrhoea is absent in most people, so no diarrhoea does not rule the infection out.
Ultrasound or CT scan of the abdomen.
A stool test for the amoeba.
A blood test for amoeba antibodies (serology). It can be normal early, so it may need repeating.
A needle drainage (aspiration) if there is no improvement in 5 to 7 days, the abscess is large or on the left side, or the diagnosis is unclear.
Your doctor will choose the treatment for the infection.
Take any prescribed medicine as directed, and ask your doctor before changing it.

sections.h: What you can do at home
items: Tell your doctor about any past travel or past residence in areas where amoebiasis is common.
Rest and drink fluids while you recover.
Your doctor may repeat blood tests or scans to check that the abscess is shrinking.
Tell your doctor if you are not better after 5 to 7 days.
This leaflet gives general information. Follow your doctor's advice.

urgent: The source entry lists no specific emergency sign for this condition.
Get urgent help if you feel suddenly much worse, or have new severe pain or confusion.

DEVICE_INFECTION.title: Infection of a central line or heart device

items: A device infection happens when germs infect a tube placed into a vein (central line) or a heart device such as a pacemaker or defibrillator.
The device may need to be removed to clear the infection.
Fever, and redness, warmth or pus at the site.
Infection in the blood (bacteraemia) that does not clear.
Blood cultures from the line and from a vein in the arm.
A tip culture if the line is removed.
An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) if there is a risk of heart valve infection.
Antibiotics are started based on the cultures.
Removing the line or device is often needed. Your team will decide.

sections.h: What you can do at home
items: Keep the site clean and dry, and tell the nurse about any redness or discharge.
Repeat blood cultures are often needed after treatment starts.
This leaflet gives general information. Follow your doctor's advice.

urgent: Fever with chills, or low blood pressure
Redness or pus at the line or device site, with pain

LEPTOSPIROSIS.title: Leptospirosis (infection from animal urine or floodwater)

items: Leptospirosis is an infection spread by the urine of infected animals, often through water or wet soil.
It usually starts 5 to 14 days after exposure.
Fever, headache, and muscle pain in the calves and back.
Red eyes (conjunctival suffusion) and sometimes jaundice (yellow skin).
Leptospira antibody tests (IgM ELISA or MAT).
Kidney and liver function tests, blood count, clotting tests, and creatine kinase (CK).
Your doctor will decide on antibiotics, and fluids or dialysis if the kidneys are affected.
Some people need admission and close monitoring.

sections.h: What you can do at home
items: Tell your doctor if you have been in floodwater or in contact with animals.
Avoid swimming in stagnant water while you are unwell.
Kidney and liver tests may be repeated to check recovery.
This leaflet gives general information. Follow your doctor's advice.

urgent: Yellow skin with confusion or drowsiness
